---
title: "Population coefficients and group variation"
execute: {warning: false, message: false}
---

The [preceding page](structured-data.qmd) identified participant and spoken word as crossed repeated units in the MALD trial table. We now separate the population associations represented by coefficients from variation across those sampled units. The [MALD data card](multiple-regression.qmd) defines response time, acoustic duration, lexical frequency, trial order, and the correct-response restriction. The [response-transformation page](response-transformations.qmd) explains why the model uses log response time. Those choices fix the measurement target before we choose a group structure.

The model uses [variance, covariance, and standard deviation](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) to describe group deviations and their relations. Conditional [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) applies only after the shared deviations are supplied. A [residual](residuals.qmd) is the remaining observed-minus-fitted response. Participant and item effects therefore require raw repeated MALD trials; they cannot be recovered from one mean per word.

We proceed from target to representation: first we name the population association, then add participant and word deviations, fit the model, and distinguish a variable's storage type from its modeling role.

## Beginning with the scientific target

We relate log response time to standardized log SUBTLEX frequency, standardized log acoustic duration, and standardized trial order. These predictors enter the population relation:

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i,\mathbf b]
=\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta
+\mathbf z_i^{\mathsf T}\mathbf b.
$$

Here $\boldsymbol\beta$ contains the population intercept and the three population associations. In particular, $\beta_{\text{frequency}}$ is the expected change in log response time for a one-standard-deviation increase in log frequency, holding duration and trial order fixed.

Here one standard deviation is computed from the retained correct-trial table used to fit the model. If $s_f$ is that sample standard deviation, then $z_{fi}=(x_{fi}-\bar x_f)/s_f$. Thus a one-unit change in `z_frequency` means an $s_f$-unit change in original log frequency, not one raw frequency unit. In a held-out prediction study, the centering and scale constants should be estimated on training data and carried into assessment data.

The word *fixed* does not mean known, measured without uncertainty, or constant across every conceivable population. It means that the coefficient is not itself indexed by a grouping level in this model.

## Representing sampled variation

Participant $p$ receives an intercept deviation and a frequency-slope deviation:

$$
\mathbf b_p=
\begin{pmatrix}b_{0p}\\b_{1p}\end{pmatrix}
\sim
\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\boldsymbol\Sigma_p).
$$

Word $w$ receives an intercept deviation,

$$
c_w\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_w^2),
$$

and the trial residual is

$$
\varepsilon_{pwi}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2).
$$

Combining the pieces gives

$$
Y_{pwi}
=\beta_0+\beta_f x_{wi}^{(f)}+\beta_d x_{wi}^{(d)}
+\beta_t x_{pwi}^{(t)}
+b_{0p}+b_{1p}x_{wi}^{(f)}+c_w+\varepsilon_{pwi}.
$$

The grouping terms follow the participant-by-word incidence structure. A participant intercept represents persistent listener speed; a word intercept represents repeated lexical-item difficulty. A participant frequency slope is requested because each participant hears words spanning frequency values and the scientific target generalizes the frequency association across listeners. An item frequency slope is not requested because a word's lexical frequency is constant across repetitions of that word. The Gaussian response and residual assumptions concern log response time conditional on these terms, and the participant, word, and residual components are assumed mutually independent unless a covariance is written explicitly.

The frequency column and participant identifier both enter the construction of the linear predictor, but they have different roles. Frequency is a measured predictor with a population coefficient. Participant identity indexes deviations drawn from a population distribution.

## Fitting the MALD model

```{r}
#| label: mald-fixed-random
library(lme4)
library(ggplot2)

mald <- read.csv("data/mald/mald-connected-trials.csv")
mald <- subset(mald, correct == 1L)

standardize <- function(x) {
  as.numeric(scale(x))
}

mald$z_frequency <- standardize(mald$log_frequency_subtlex)
mald$z_duration <- standardize(mald$log_duration)
mald$z_trial <- standardize(mald$trial_order)

fit <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ z_frequency + z_duration + z_trial +
    (1 + z_frequency | participant_id) +
    (1 | item),
  data = mald,
  control = lmerControl(
    optimizer = "bobyqa",
    optCtrl = list(maxfun = 200000L)
  )
)

data.frame(
  term = names(lme4::fixef(fit)),
  estimate = unname(lme4::fixef(fit)),
  row.names = NULL
)
```

The formula maps term by term onto the mathematical model:

| `lmer` term | Mathematical role |
|---|---|
| `z_frequency + z_duration + z_trial` | population coefficients $\beta_f,\beta_d,\beta_t$ |
| `(1 + z_frequency \| participant_id)` | correlated participant deviations $(b_{0p},b_{1p})$ |
| `(1 \| item)` | word intercept $c_w$ |
| implicit Gaussian residual | $\varepsilon_{pwi}$ |

`bobyqa` is a derivative-free optimizer used here for the variance parameters, and `maxfun = 200000` raises the evaluation budget for the correlated slope model. These settings address computation; they do not change the probability model or repair an unsupported grouping term.

The fitted frequency coefficient is `r sprintf("%.3f", lme4::fixef(fit)[["z_frequency"]])` log-response-time units per standard deviation. This is a population association conditional on duration and trial order. It is not a participant-specific slope or a causal effect of lexical frequency.

## Showing raw data and the fitted population relation

Plotting all trials would obscure the relation. We thus summarize the raw responses in empirical frequency bins and draw the fitted population line at mean duration and mean trial order.

```{r}
#| label: plot-mald-fixed-random
frequency_breaks <- unique(quantile(
  mald$z_frequency,
  probs = seq(0, 1, length.out = 13L),
  names = FALSE
))
mald$frequency_bin <- cut(
  mald$z_frequency,
  breaks = frequency_breaks,
  include.lowest = TRUE
)

raw_bins <- aggregate(
  cbind(z_frequency, log_rt) ~ frequency_bin,
  data = mald,
  FUN = mean
)

prediction_grid <- data.frame(
  z_frequency = seq(
    min(raw_bins$z_frequency),
    max(raw_bins$z_frequency),
    length.out = 160L
  ),
  z_duration = 0,
  z_trial = 0
)
prediction_grid$fitted_log_rt <- predict(
  fit,
  newdata = prediction_grid,
  re.form = NA
)

ggplot(raw_bins, aes(x = z_frequency, y = log_rt)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey35", size = 1.8) +
  geom_line(
    data = prediction_grid,
    aes(y = fitted_log_rt),
    color = "#1F5A85",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "SUBTLEX log frequency (standardized)",
    y = "Log response time"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

The points are raw bin means; the line sets participant and item deviations to zero. Thus it describes the fitted population relation on the same response scale, not the trajectory of an observed participant or word.

## Storage type does not determine modeling role

Frequency, participant, item, and part of speech can all be stored as columns. Their storage types do not decide whether they receive population coefficients or group distributions. The decision follows the estimand and sampling design. A measured property that encodes a theoretical contrast belongs in the population relation. A sampled identifier that records repeated observations can index remaining variation around that relation.

The course formula omits controls analyzed by Tucker et al. It isolates the covariance concepts needed here and does not reproduce their predictor comparison.

## Recap and check

1. Why is there a participant frequency slope but no item frequency slope? Frequency varies within participants but is constant within each word.
2. Does “fixed effect” mean known without uncertainty? No. It is an estimated population coefficient that is not indexed by a grouping level in this model.

The [next page](random-effects.qmd) shows how the group distributions produce partial pooling.
